say: The Chemistry Behind Liquid Products. This is module 1 of the course.
Three tools first: which surfactant does which job, how pH works, and how to keep germs out.

shots.label: Surfactant stirred into water
say: Look at this bucket. We're stirring a surfactant into water, gently.
Each surfactant molecule has a head that loves water and a tail that loves oil.
The tails gather into tiny balls called micelles. Grease slips inside, and the rinse water carries it away.

shots.label: Four surfactant families

card.title: The four families
card.note: Grouped by the charge on the head

say: On this shelf they're grouped by the charge on the head.
Anionics like SLES clean and foam. CAPB makes them milder. Nonionics cut grease. Cationics disinfect, condition hair and soften fabric.

shots.label: Fabric softener (cationic)
shots.banner: Never mix anionic cleaners with cationics
say: This milky liquid is fabric softener, a cationic product.
Anionic and cationic surfactants attract each other and form a sticky solid that does neither job.
That's why softener goes in the rinse, not with the detergent.

shots.label: SLES paste, about 70% active
say: Watch the scale as we scoop in SLES paste. It's commonly about 70% active, so 100 g holds about 70 g of real surfactant.
CAPB is usually around 30% active. Always read your supplier's data sheet, because the figure changes.
Here's Bisi's sum. Active matter is the percentage you use times its strength, added up.
Her formula is 12.3% active, 615 g of real surfactant in 5 kg.
When her new SLES was only 60% active, she used 875 g instead of 750 g to keep the same strength.

shots.label: Universal indicator strip
say: This strip reads pH, from 0 to 14. Water is 7. Below is acidic, above is alkaline, and each step is ten times stronger.
Dip, wait the time on the pack, and compare the colour in daylight. Test before you add dye.

shots.label: Gloves and goggles
shots.banner: Add acid or caustic slowly TO water
say: Before making any adjuster solution, put on gloves and goggles.
Add acid or caustic slowly to water, never water onto the chemical, because heat and splashing can result. Label every adjuster bottle.

shots.label: 200 g sample in a clean cup

card.title: Amaka's 20 kg shampoo
card.note: Adjust the sample first, then the batch

say: Amaka weighed a 200 g sample, 1% of her batch, and added citric solution in drops until it read pH 6. That took 0.9 g.
Times 100 gives 90 g. She added 72 g first, tested, then the rest slowly, so she never overshot.

shots.label: Toilet cleaner and bleach
say: When you test products at home, keep the toilet cleaner and the bleach apart, just like these two bottles.

shots.label: Boiled, cooled water
say: Liquid soap is mostly water, and water feeds germs. So use treated water, or water boiled and cooled covered.
Wash drums and paddles, rinse, wipe with 70% alcohol and let them dry. Never use them for food.

shots.label: Preservative (phenoxyethanol blend)
say: A preservative stops germs that get in later. Hauwa checked her pH was in the supplier's range, then weighed 200 g on a digital scale.
Add it below about 40 degrees Celsius, because heat can damage some preservatives. And avoid formalin: it is toxic.

shots.label: New, sanitised bottles
say: Now fill into new or sanitised bottles, then cap and label quickly.

shots.label: Retained samples: room and warm
say: Keep two bottles from every batch, one at room temperature, one somewhere warm.
Check them weekly for four weeks, then monthly: smell, colour, clarity, thickness, pH and swelling.

shots.label: Eyewash bottle of clean water
say: Read the Safety Data Sheet for every chemical. Wear nitrile gloves and goggles, ventilate, and keep an eyewash bottle of clean water nearby, like this one.
Now go through the lessons below. Build your raw material register, map the pH of five products at home, and set up your clean corner.
